topics.title: Developing Frontend Applications
topics.content: UfitGo consists of three main frontends: a React Native Expo mobile app, a Next.js user website, and a Vite-powered React admin console. These clients share business concepts but evolve independently.
topics.resolution: Action: When building a new user-facing flow, always check if the concept needs to be implemented across mobile, web, and admin. Do not assume one frontend is the only source of truth.

topics.title: Building in the Primary Backends
topics.content: Our main transactional APIs are modular NestJS services written in TypeScript. The user API handles wallet, savings, and KYC. Separate NestJS services run the admin and operator experiences.
topics.resolution: Action: Place new business logic inside the service that actually owns the domain boundary. Do not duplicate domain logic across the admin, operator, or API gateway layers.

topics.title: Integrating with Go Services
topics.content: The `payment-service` and `notification-service` are written in Go. `payment-service` manages gateway debits and background worker modes. `notification-service` handles all outbound emails and messages.
topics.resolution: Action: If your new feature requires payment execution or sending emails/SMS, integrate with these existing Go services via API calls instead of building that workload directly into the NestJS user API.

topics.title: Managing the Persistence Layer
topics.content: PostgreSQL is our system of record (users, savings, wallet balances). TypeORM is the standard data access layer in NestJS. Redis is used for caching and shared state.
topics.resolution: Action: Always implement schema changes using explicit TypeORM entities and migration scripts. Use DTO validation for all inputs. Avoid storing ad-hoc JSON blobs.

topics.title: Working with Banking-as-a-Service
topics.content: We provision virtual accounts via BaaS integrations (e.g. Wema/FCMB). The `baas_accounts` table links provider-specific accounts to our users, allowing deposits to be matched to wallets and constrained by KYC limits.
topics.resolution: Action: If you need to swap or add a BaaS provider, implement it behind the existing internal abstraction. This ensures wallet funding and compliance checks remain untouched.

topics.title: Handling KYC Providers
topics.content: Identity verification (BVN, NIN, liveness) is handled dynamically by our KYC subsystem. We are currently in a hybrid state where legacy user KYC fields coexist with the newer profile models.
topics.resolution: Action: When updating KYC flows, ensure you update both the legacy KYC records and the new KYC profile models until the migration is officially completed.

topics.title: Configuring Payment Gateways & Webhooks
topics.content: External gateways (Paystack, Monnify) handle card funding and debits. Webhooks are critical for finalizing wallet/savings states after a gateway event.
topics.resolution: Action: Always ensure gateway webhooks are signature-validated and idempotent. If you alter payment success logic, test both the direct API return path and the asynchronous webhook path.

topics.title: Triggering Notifications
topics.content: The user API dictates *when* a notification should fire, but the Go `notification-service` handles the actual template delivery.
topics.resolution: Action: To debug missing emails, first check the user API logs to see if the trigger fired. If it did, check the `notification-service` logs for delivery failures.

topics.title: Managing the Auto-Debit Worker
topics.content: Recurring auto-debits run via the `payment-service` Docker image in a dedicated worker mode (set via `APP_MODE`), triggered by EventBridge.
topics.resolution: Action: Do not add scheduled financial tasks to the NestJS API. Any critical scheduled financial work must run as an explicit worker task.

topics.title: Creating Safe In-App Cron Jobs
topics.content: Jobs like KYC monitoring and savings auditing run inside the user API. Because the API scales horizontally, these jobs use PostgreSQL advisory locks (via `CronLockService`) to prevent duplicate executions.
topics.resolution: Action: If you add a new cron job to the user API, you MUST wrap it in a distributed lock before executing its logic, or it will run multiple times in production.

topics.title: Triggering Savings Reminders
topics.content: Savings reminders are triggered by an external scheduler calling a protected endpoint in the user API, guarded by `x-system-key`.
topics.resolution: Action: To manually test or wire up new schedulers for reminders, call this protected system task endpoint rather than bypassing the API boundary.

topics.title: Monitoring Job Observability
topics.content: All background jobs must emit structured logs including duration and processed record counts to help operators detect silent failures.
topics.resolution: Action: Before deploying a new scheduled job, ensure it logs its execution time and the number of items it processed. A job is not production-ready without these metrics.

topics.title: Enforcing Modular Domain Ownership
topics.content: Our codebase uses strict domain boundaries (Wallet, Savings, KYC, Notifications). Each module owns its own controllers and persistence logic.
topics.resolution: Action: Fix bugs and add business rules in the service/module that actually owns the data. Do not patch logic in gateways or downstream consumers.

topics.title: Using Environment-Driven Modes
topics.content: We use runtime flags (like `APP_MODE` in `payment-service`) to switch behaviors between HTTP API and background worker within the same codebase.
topics.resolution: Action: Only use explicit environment-driven modes if both modes share the same code ownership. Otherwise, split them into cleanly separated codebases.

topics.title: Defining Internal API Contracts
topics.content: Services communicate via internal HTTP APIs protected by shared secrets (e.g., `x-internal-api-key`).
topics.resolution: Action: When Service A needs data from Service B, create a protected endpoint in Service B. NEVER connect Service A directly to Service B's database.

topics.title: Implementing Progressive Compliance
topics.content: We use Progressive KYC: users start with minimal friction (Tier 1) and are prompted for deeper compliance (Tier 2/3) only when their balance or risk profile grows.
topics.resolution: Action: When building new high-risk financial features, tie them into the progressive KYC state rather than building standalone compliance checks.

topics.title: Routing via Application Load Balancer (ALB)
topics.content: Traffic to `api.ufitgo.ng` hits an AWS ALB, which routes requests to backend services based on path rules. The ALB path map is the single source of truth.
topics.resolution: Action: If an endpoint returns 503, do not assume the app is down. First check the ALB listener rules and target-group health in AWS.

topics.title: Understanding Public Route Families
topics.content: Public API routing is strictly defined: `/api/health` for User API, `/api/v1/*` for Payment Service, etc.
topics.resolution: Action: When debugging frontend connection issues, verify the exact route being called matches our ALB rules. A healthy service behind a misconfigured route appears as an outage.

topics.title: Deploying ECS Express Services
topics.content: Core APIs are deployed as independent ECS Express services with individual task definitions and health checks.
topics.resolution: Action: Treat the ECS service health, the Target Group health, and the ALB routing rules as three separate points of failure during production debugging.

topics.title: Managing Secrets and Configuration
topics.content: We use AWS SSM Parameter Store and Secrets Manager for sensitive config. Local `.env` files are for development only.
topics.resolution: Action: When investigating production behavior, never rely on your local `.env`. Verify the actual runtime config injected into the ECS task.

topics.title: Creating Operational Runbooks
topics.content: Background jobs and new infrastructure require explicit operational ownership, including CloudWatch alarms and runbooks.
topics.resolution: Action: When shipping a new scheduler or worker, you must include setup scripts, CloudWatch alarm definitions, and rollback instructions in the PR.
